html:
The Battle of Stalingrad was fought from August 1942 to 2 February 1943 in and around Stalingrad, now Volgograd, on the Volga in southern Russia. The Red Army surrounded and destroyed the German Sixth Army. It was the turning point of World War II in Europe.

After failing at Moscow, Germany attacked in the south in 1942 to seize the oil of the Caucasus. Taking Stalingrad would cut the Volga. The city also bore Stalin's name, and neither he nor Hitler would let go. German bombing wrecked it in August. For three months the two armies fought for single factories and houses, the Soviet defenders holding a thin strip along the river. On 19 November the Soviet command struck the weak Romanian armies on both flanks and in four days trapped over 250,000 men. Hitler forbade a breakout. Supply by air failed, and a relief attack was stopped. Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus surrendered.

About 91,000 Germans went into captivity, and only about 5,000 ever came home. The two sides together lost perhaps two million killed, wounded and captured, one of the highest tolls of any battle in history. After Kursk the next summer, it only retreated.
